passages.happening:
The first lot falls to the tribe of Judah. The writer walks its borders one side at a time.

The southern border runs through the dry country at the edge of Edom, by the Wilderness of Zin, and out to the sea (verses 1-4). The eastern border is the Salt Sea, as far north as the mouth of the Jordan (verse 5). The northern border climbs from the Jordan into the hills, passes along the Valley of Hinnom on the south side of Jerusalem, and runs down to the coast (verses 5-11). The western border is the Great Sea (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Judah comes first, and its account is by far the longest of any tribe. Judah was the tribe of the kings who would later rule from Jerusalem. For generations of readers these were the borders of home.

Borders in the ancient world were not lines on paper. They were drawn from one landmark to the next: a spring, a ridge, a valley, a notable stone, a town. A person could walk a border and know where one family's land ended and another's began. The word ‘border’ comes more than twenty times in this chapter.

That matters because of what a border protected. Each family's land was its living and its place among God's people. The law forbade anyone to move a neighbor's boundary stone. A border was a guard set around the share God had given to someone else.

Judah's land was very mixed. It held the dry Negev in the south, the low hills toward the coast, the high country around Hebron, and the bare slopes that fall away to the Salt Sea, which is the Dead Sea.

One name on the northern border has a long later history. The Valley of Hinnom, beside Jerusalem, became in later centuries a place where children were sacrificed to other gods, and the prophets condemned it. Its name, in the form Gehenna, became a word Jesus used for final judgment.

These verses record the shares of ancient tribes. They are not a guide to any border today, and these notes do not use them as one.
passages.later:
The law that guarded such borders reads, “You must not move your neighbor’s boundary marker, which was set up by your ancestors to mark the inheritance you shall receive in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess” (Deuteronomy 19:14).

Jacob, long before, had said of this tribe, “The scepter will not depart from Judah” (Genesis 49:10).
passages.asks: Israel's law treated a neighbor's boundary as something to protect and never to shift. Ask where you press on the edges of what belongs to others: their time, their property, their good name, their place. And ask whether you are content inside the lines that have fallen to you, or always looking over them.

passages.happening:
The story of Caleb, begun in the last chapter, is finished here. Joshua gives him Hebron, as God commanded. “And Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak” (verse 14).

Then Caleb marches on the town of Debir, and makes an offer: “To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage” (verse 16). Othniel, the son of Caleb's brother Kenaz, takes the town and marries her.

One day Acsah urges her husband to ask her father for a field. Then she rides to Caleb herself. When she gets down from her donkey, he asks, “What do you desire?” (verse 18).

“Give me a blessing,” she answered. “Since you have given me land in the Negev, give me springs of water as well.” And Caleb gives her the upper springs and the lower springs (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Caleb had said in chapter 14, ‘Perhaps with the LORD’s help I will drive them out’. This passage reports that he did. The people whose size had frightened a generation out of the land are moved out of Hebron by a man of eighty-five.

The offer of a daughter to the man who takes a city sounds strange now. In that world it was a way to honor a champion, and fathers arranged their children's marriages as a matter of course. It is not a pattern for anyone today. The text simply reports it. The man who wins is Othniel, who will appear again in the book of Judges as the first of Israel's judges.

The part of the story the writer lingers on is Acsah. The land she had been given was in the Negev, the dry south. Land there without water was close to useless. She sees what is missing and goes to get it. First she presses her husband to ask. Then she goes herself.

Her father's question is open: ‘What do you desire?’ And her request is direct. She asks for a gift, and names it: springs. Caleb gives more than she named, the upper springs and the lower ones too.

So in the middle of a long chapter of borders and town lists stands a short scene in which a daughter asks her father plainly for what she needs and receives it gladly. The same story is told again at the start of Judges. In a book much concerned with inheritance, this is what receiving one looks like.

Debir is said in chapter 10 to have been destroyed by Joshua. Here it has to be taken again. The book does not explain how the two fit, and many readers take it as a sign that the summaries of chapter 10 are not to be pressed too far.
passages.later:
The book of Judges tells the same story and then says what became of Othniel: “But when the Israelites cried out to the LORD, He raised up Othniel son of Caleb’s younger brother Kenaz as a deliverer to save them” (Judges 3:9).

Jesus speaks of a Father who gives when he is asked: “So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!” (Matthew 7:11).
passages.asks: Acsah knew what her land lacked, and she asked her father for it without a speech. Ask what is missing from what you have been given, without which the rest will not bear fruit. Ask whether you have named it to God as plainly as she named the springs. And if someone depends on you, ask whether they would feel free to get down from the donkey and ask.

passages.t: The towns of Judah, and Jerusalem
passages.happening:
“This is the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Judah” (verse 20).

What follows is a list of towns, set out by region. First the towns of the Negev in the far south, toward Edom (verses 21-32). Then the towns of the foothills (verses 33-47). Then the towns of the hill country (verses 48-60). Last, a handful in the wilderness by the Salt Sea, among them En-gedi (verses 61-62). After each group the writer gives a total and adds that the towns came ‘along with their villages’.

The last verse is of another kind. “But the descendants of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem. So to this day the Jebusites live there among the descendants of Judah” (verse 63).
passages.hearers:
This is the kind of passage a new reader is tempted to skip, and it is fair to read it quickly. But it is worth knowing what it is.

It is a register of property. For a family in Judah, finding its own town in this list was like finding its name on a deed. The repeated words ‘along with their villages’ matter. A walled town was the market and the place of safety for the small farming settlements around it. Most Israelites lived in those unnamed villages, and the phrase makes sure they are counted.

Some of the totals do not match the number of names. That is probably because some names are double names, or because the list was brought up to date as it was copied.

Scholars debate where the list came from. Some hold that it reflects the districts of the later kingdom of Judah. Others hold that it keeps older tribal records, updated over time.

Several towns here have stories still to come. David will hide from Saul at En-gedi and will be given Ziklag. Lachish and Azekah will be among the last towns of Judah to hold out when Babylon invades, centuries later.

Then comes verse 63. After sixty verses of towns received, the chapter ends with one town not taken. The people of Jerusalem stayed where they were. The writer says so without excuse. The Jebusites lived on there until David took the city, generations afterward. The words ‘to this day’ show that when this sentence was written, that had not yet happened.

It is like the book to end its fullest chapter this way. It will not let the reader think the gift had been fully received.
passages.later:
The book of Judges says the same of the neighboring tribe: “The Benjamites, however, failed to drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem” (Judges 1:21).

David's capture of the city is told in 2 Samuel: “Nevertheless, David captured the fortress of Zion (that is, the City of David)” (2 Samuel 5:7).

The prophet Micah named one small town of Judah's hills for a greater future: “But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel” (Micah 5:2). Matthew quotes that promise when he tells of the birth of Jesus (Matthew 2:6).
passages.asks: The writer counted the small villages with the towns, and he ended an account of great gain with one honest line about what was not done. Ask who the unnamed ‘villages’ are in your church or your work, the people who are rarely listed, and whether you count them. And ask whether you can tell the story of your own life with its verse 63 left in.
